questions.prompt: What does copy-on-write mean for what a shadow copy actually stores?
options: A complete duplicate of the volume at snapshot time
Only the blocks that have changed since the snapshot, making snapshots relatively cheap so several can coexist
A compressed archive of the whole disk
questions.explanation: Because only changed blocks are preserved, multiple snapshots covering weeks of history can exist on a normal workstation without consuming proportional storage.

questions.prompt: What is the underused registry-diff technique this lesson describes?
options: Extracting a hive from a pre-intrusion shadow copy and diffing it against the current hive, producing a persistence inventory by comparison
questions.explanation: Every added Run key, service, and modified value appears as a difference -- turning persistence hunting into a comparison exercise rather than a search.

questions.prompt: Why is bulk shadow copy deletion such a high-confidence indicator?
options: Normal operation and routine administration do not delete shadow copies at scale, making it a near-universal pre-encryption ransomware precursor
questions.explanation: Because it removes the victim's recovery path, it is frequently the last clear signal before encryption deploys -- and one of the most valuable things to alert on in real time.

questions.prompt: Why can't shadow copy history be relied upon to always exist?
options: Snapshots are deleted automatically under storage pressure, oldest first, and may be disabled entirely by policy
They are stored only in memory
They require a domain controller to maintain
questions.explanation: Storage-driven automatic deletion means available history varies by system and cannot be assumed without checking.
